newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany against weakening EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany against weakening EMU criteria.

text.p: Germany on Wednesday insisted the economic criteria for membership of Europe's single currency must not be softened and said economic and monetary union (EMU) would go ahead on time.
Both Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel set out Germany's line after a cabinet meeting on Europe ahead of next week's European Union summit in Dublin.
They said EMU should begin in 1999, as set down in the Maastricht Treaty, and only countries which meet the fiscal targets in the treaty should be allowed to participate.

"The German government stands without reservation for realising economic and monetary union at the pre-agreed time and sticking to the criteria agreed in the treaty," Kohl said at a reception for foreign diplomats in Bonn.
Kinkel said any change in plans for the currency, the euro, would hurt its acceptance by financial markets and the people of the 15-nation European Union.
"The euro must, as agreed in Maastricht, come on January 1, 1999. A delay is not an option and any softening of the criteria is out of the question," he said in a statement.
"At the European Council meeting in Dublin in a few days, we want to push forward the process of European unity," Kohl said.
"The excellent Franco-German cooperation, based on the strong friendship between our two countries, will prove itself to be the engine in this process once again."
Kinkel said it was necessary to "close the holes" in the Maastricht Treaty that set out the framework for EMU by agreeing a "stability pact" among countries taking part.
"Monetary union is only conceivable as a community of stability," he said. "Therefore we must back up budget discipline in the EU member states with a stability pact."
Kinkel added that Germany and France would outline the details of a joint initiative on EMU at a Franco-German summit next week ahead of the Dublin conference.
